extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy, and the theory of reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and analytic framework for the preliminary stages of formal logic: the role of language, the nature and classification of names, and the structure of propositions as foundation for judging evidence and correct inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Logic (science of operations subservient to estimation of evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Logic, then, is the science of the operations of the understanding which are subservient to the estimation of evidence: both the process itself of advancing from known truths to unknown, and all other intellectual operations in so far as auxiliary to this."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes explicitly the operations of Naming, Definition, and Classification because language is an instrument of thought; places logic as concerned primarily with matters resolved by evidence rather than direct consciousness; emphasizes logic's role as judge of inferences drawn from evidence in any science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of logical inquiry: analyse inference and frame canons for testing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our object, then, will be, to attempt a correct analysis of the intellectual process called Reasoning or Inference, and of such other mental operations as are intended to facilitate this: as well as, on the foundation of this analysis, and pari passu with it, to bring together or frame a set of rules or canons for testing the sufficiency of any given evidence to prove any given proposition."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practical aim is both descriptive (analyze reasoning) and prescriptive (produce canons/rules for testing sufficiency of evidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit principle for analysis (only so far as necessary for practical discrimination)
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis of mental operations should be carried only "so far as may be requisite for ascertaining the difference between a correct and an incorrect performance of those processes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not pursue decomposition into ultimate elements beyond the point where inaccuracies would be detectable in reasoning practice; analogy: anatomy of muscles need be studied only insofar as it affects practical use or cure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of commencing with analysis of language
rubrics_metrics.description: Because reasoning usually takes place by means of words, "those who have not a thorough insight into the signification and purposes of words, will be under chances, amounting almost to certainty, of reasoning or inferring incorrectly."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language analysis is a necessary preliminary to logic: understand meaning/use of words to avoid confusion; analogy to learning to adjust optical instruments before astronomical observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition as the primary object of inquiry and its three-part structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition is "discourse, in which something is affirmed or denied of something." Every proposition consists of Subject, Predicate, and Copula (the sign denoting affirmation or denial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Gold is yellow' (predicate = yellow; subject = gold; copula = is). Investigating propositions informs what questions can be asked and what answers can be given in inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum compositional requirement of a proposition: two names/objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the simplest act of belief "supposes, and has something to do with, two objects—two names...two namable things." The example contrasts 'the sun' (no belief) with 'the sun exists' (invokes existence as a second object).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that belief and propositional content require at least two distinct objects or concepts (e.g., subject and existence or predicate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Function and proper reference of names (names of things, not merely ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: A name is a word serving to recall a thought and to make it known to others; when used to express belief a name refers to the thing itself "not merely of our ideas of things."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument (via Hobbes) and examples clarify that when saying 'the sun is the cause of day' we refer to physical facts (things), not merely to ideas; thus treat words as names of things intended in assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between words that are names and parts of names (categorematic vs syncategorematic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some words (particles like 'of', inflected cases, adverbs) are not names and cannot stand as subject/predicate except when referring to the word itself; such words are 'syncategorematic'. Words that can stand alone as subject or predicate are 'categorematic'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjectives can sometimes function as names by ellipsis (e.g., 'White is an agreeable color'); many-worded names (mixed terms) may be treated as single categorematic terms in logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for whether a multiword phrase is one name or multiple names (predication test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mode of determining whether any set of words makes only one name is by predicating something of it and observing whether, by this predication, we make only one assertion. If only one assertion results, the phrase counts as one name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'John Nokes, who was the mayor of the town, died yesterday' counts as one name (one assertion of dying), whereas 'John Nokes and the mayor of the town died yesterday' makes two assertions (two names).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary classification: general (common) names vs individual (singular) names
rubrics_metrics.description: A general name is 'capable of being truly affirmed, in the same sense, of each of an indefinite number of things' (e.g., 'man'); an individual or singular name is capable of being truly affirmed of one thing only (e.g., 'John').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General names support universal predication across many individuals; singular names do not indicate qualities common to many and thus are not predicable in the same sense across individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of collective names from general names
rubrics_metrics.description: A collective name (e.g., 'the 76th regiment of foot') can be predicated only of the group taken together, not of each member separately; hence it is collective but not necessarily general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast 'the 76th regiment' (collective, not predicable of individual soldiers) with 'a regiment' (both collective and general with respect to individual regiments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Division into concrete and abstract names
rubrics_metrics.description: A concrete name stands for a thing (e.g., 'John', 'the sea'); an abstract name stands for an attribute (e.g., 'whiteness').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains historical/scholastic usage versus later practices that misuse 'abstract' to mean all generalized names; recommends using 'abstract' as name of attributes and 'concrete' as name of objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: When abstract names are general or neither (treatment of attribute-names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some abstract names are general (e.g., 'color', or 'whiteness' used across shades); others designate a single attribute (e.g., 'visibleness', 'tangibleness') and may be neither general nor individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposes avoiding logomachy by possibly placing such singular-attribute abstract names in a separate class rather than forcing them into 'general' or 'individual' categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction to connotative vs non-connotative distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: The text announces a third great division of names into 'connotative' and 'non-connotative' (the latter sometimes called 'absolute').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At this point the distinction is introduced; fuller explanation follows subsequently. This flags another principal classificatory criterion for names to be examined.
